Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the data patterns:

## Example 1 (2024-12-06)
- History: Price range ~66.3 to 70.0, generally trending up
- Sentiment: Mix of positive (0.67, 1.00) and neutral/negative
- Model forecasts: Start around 68.26, 66.22, 67.98...
- True outcomes: 68.31, 66.37, 68.18, 68.63, 66.10, 64.43, 64.26, 64.86, 67.69, 68.20, 69.68, 69.47, 71.56, 71.98, 73.00, 75.19, 75.94, 74.36, 74.04, 72.17, 65.32, 65.69, 66.35, 67.50, 67.16, 67.52, 67.44, 67.89, 68.23, 68.33

Looking at the divergence pattern:
- Early horizons (days 1-7): Model is too low compared to outcomes
- Days 8-12: Model catches up but still slightly low
- Days 13-20: Model is significantly too low - outcomes are 10-15 points higher
- Days 21-25: Model is again too low by ~5-10 points
- Days 26-30: Model is too low by ~3-8 points

Wait, let me look at this more carefully. The outcomes show a clear upward trend that accelerates. The model seems to be under-predicting this acceleration.

Looking at Example 2 (2024-12-11):
- Very similar pattern - model forecasts are consistently below outcomes


- Early horizons show a 0.5-1.0 point difference
- Middle horizons diverge by 2-3 points
- Later horizons extend to 4-6 point discrepancies

I notice a consistent pattern of model forecasts being lower than true outcomes, with divergence increasing across different time horizons. The sentiment history might provide additional insights into these systematic deviations.

Analyzing sentiment markers reveals complex market dynamics. Positive sentiment peaks at 1.00, indicating strong bullish sentiment,
